title: The talkative tortoise
hookLine: two geese carry a tortoise on a stick; he opens his mouth to answer the jeers and falls (Jataka 215)

lines: A KING WHO TALKED TOO MUCH.
A TORTOISE FALLS FROM THE SKY.
cards: A comeback, typed and ready. A thumb hovering over send. Someone in the comments said something smug, and the reply is right there.
Hold that moment. There was once a king of Benares, the story goes, who talked too much. Nobody else could get a word in.
His wise adviser, who tradition says was the Buddha in an earlier life, had been waiting for a way to tell him so without getting in trouble.
Then one day a tortoise fell out of the sky and landed in the palace courtyard, split in two. The king asked how on earth that happened, and the adviser told him.

teach.h: A STICK, TWO GEESE, ONE TORTOISE.
teach.b: Up in the mountains, a tortoise lived in a lake, and two young wild geese used to come there to feed. They became friends. Come home with us, the geese said.
We live in a golden cave in the Himalayas. It's beautiful. How? said the tortoise.
I can't fly. The geese had an idea: we'll hold the two ends of a stick in our beaks, you bite down on the middle, and we'll fly you there. Just one thing.
Keep your mouth shut the whole way. Not a word. Off they go, a goose at each end, the tortoise clamped on the middle.
Over a village, the children look up and shout: look, look! Two geese carrying a tortoise on a stick! The tortoise gets angry.
He wants to say: if my friends want to carry me, what's it to you, you brats?

teach.h: HE OPENS HIS MOUTH TO ANSWER.
teach.b: He opens his mouth to say it, lets go of the stick, and down he falls, right into the king's courtyard. The adviser turns to the king and says, gently: this is what happens to people who can't hold their tongue.
The Jataka says the king understood the story was about him, and from then on he spoke less.
The good thing here: the tortoise isn't wicked. He isn't even wrong; the kids really were being rude. He just couldn't let it go unanswered, and that one reply cost him everything.
The same story is told in other Indian fable collections too, like the Panchatantra. The tortoise could be anyone with a thumb over send.

how: The talkative tortoise is told to children in Buddhist homes and schools, and Buddhist teaching counts right speech, including knowing when not to speak, as part of the eightfold path.

games.q: you're the tortoise, flying high on a stick. kids below are shouting and laughing at you. what do you do?
o: ask the geese to fly higher.
games.why: he opens his mouth to tell them off, lets go of the stick, and falls into the king's courtyard.

practice: Remember a moment when someone said something that stung and you wanted to fire back, and feel the words line up, ready to go.
Now, like the tortoise on the stick, keep your mouth closed and breathe through your nose, letting the words stay unspoken. Notice that you're still flying.

wordCard.voice: Kacchapa. The tortoise carried through the sky on a stick by two geese, who opened his mouth to answer the jeers, and fell.

orig.note: Pali: tortoise, turtle. The story is the Kacchapa Jataka.

carryVoice: Your line: not every word needs saying. One reply, and he let go of the stick. Day eighty-seven, in the books.
